lines.text: Configuration from a position, or the reverse → walk the periods: in period $n$ the s-block fills $n$s, the d-block $(n-1)$d and the p-block $n$p; period = highest occupied level; group = outer s and d electrons in the d-block, or valence electrons (plus 10 in the p-block; helium is group 18); Cr and Cu are $\mathrm{4s^{1}}$ ({{lesson:3.1}})

Explain a trend in radius, ionization energy, electron affinity or group 1 and 17 reactivity → nuclear charge, occupied levels (distance) and shielding, then the attraction on the outer electrons: across a period the nuclear charge wins, down a group distance and shielding win ({{lesson:3.1}}, {{lesson:3.2}})
Halogen added to a halide solution → it reacts only if the halogen is above the halide in group 17; give the ionic equation, such as $\ce{Cl2(aq) + 2Br^-(aq) -> 2Cl^-(aq) + Br2(aq)}$ ({{lesson:3.2}})

Oxide with water, or acidic or basic? → group 1 and 2 oxides (ionic) are basic, $\ce{O^2- + H2O -> 2OH^-}$; non-metal oxides (covalent) are acidic: $\ce{SO2}$ gives $\ce{H2SO3}$, $\ce{SO3}$ gives $\ce{H2SO4}$, $\ce{CO2}$ gives $\ce{H2CO3}$; $\ce{Al2O3}$ is amphoteric, $\ce{CO}$ and $\ce{NO}$ are neutral ({{lesson:3.2}})

Oxidation state of an atom → oxidation states add up to the overall charge; use the fixed values first (F $-1$, group 1 $+1$, group 2 $+2$, Al $+3$), then H $+1$ and O $-2$; H is $-1$ in metal hydrides and O $-1$ in peroxides; write the sign first ({{lesson:3.3}})

Molecular formula from a skeletal or general formula → a carbon at every corner and line end, H to give each carbon four bonds, then the atoms written in; for the $n$th member of a series, count from its smallest molecule (ethene for alkenes) ({{lesson:3.6}})

Name a compound, or find all its structural isomers → longest chain containing the functional group; lowest locant to the suffix group, then C=C, then prefixes in alphabetical order; for isomers, shorten the straight chain one carbon at a time and name each, since a repeated name is a repeated compound ({{lesson:3.7}})

Explain a dip in first ionization energy (group 2 to 13, or 15 to 16) → the electron removed is in a higher-energy sublevel (p after s) or is paired and repelled, so less energy is needed; not the stability of full or half-full sublevels ({{lesson:3.4}})

Configuration of a transition-metal ion → write the atom first (Cr $\mathrm{[Ar]\,4s^{1}\,3d^{5}}$, Cu $\mathrm{[Ar]\,4s^{1}\,3d^{10}}$), then remove 4s electrons before 3d. Charge of a complex → metal ion's charge plus the ligands' charges, with $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{NH3}$ neutral ({{lesson:3.4}})

Is a complex coloured, and what colour? → it needs a partly filled 3d sublevel ($\mathrm{3d^{1}}$ to $\mathrm{3d^{9}}$) and a gap matching visible light; the colour seen is opposite the colour absorbed on the wheel (data booklet, section 15); $\Delta E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$ with $\lambda$ in metres, so a larger splitting absorbs a shorter wavelength ({{lesson:3.5}})

Does it have stereoisomers? → cis-trans needs restricted rotation (C=C or a small ring) and two different groups on each of the two carbons; a molecule with one chiral carbon (four different atoms or groups) has two enantiomers ({{lesson:3.8}})

Identify an unknown from spectra → MS: $\ce{M+}$ gives $M_\text{r}$, mass lost from section 22; IR: bonds from section 20 (alcohol O–H broad 3200–3600, acid O–H very broad 2500–3000, C=O 1700–1750 $\pu{cm-1}$); $^{1}\ce{H}$ NMR: signals = environments, integration = hydrogen ratio, $n$ neighbouring H give $n + 1$ peaks; check every datum ({{lesson:3.9}}, {{lesson:3.10}})
